title: [R-835] ストレイントロニクス：歪みによる新奇物性発現：[R-836] 原子層堆積（ALD）のはじまりと発展
When AI takes control, who takes responsibility? Structural analysis of agentic AI risks in supply chains
abstract: Purpose Agentic AI systems execute procurement decisions, reroute shipments and renegotiate supplier contracts at speeds that preclude real-time human review. The existing literature offers limited analytical attention to the risks that arise when decision authority is delegated to agents. This paper develops a risk taxonomy for agentic AI in supply chains and traces the hierarchical dependencies and influence magnitudes among the identified risks. Design/methodology/approach A systematic review of literature, analyzed through theories–characteristics–contexts–methods framework, produces the risk taxonomy. A hybrid modified total interpretive structural modeling and fuzzy decision-making trial and evaluation laboratory methodology is then applied to structured expert judgments to establish the causal hierarchy and quantify inter-risk influence. Findings Three risks, namely workforce skill gap, data quality and reliability and ethical misalignment occupy the deepest level of the causal hierarchy. Lack of accountability and governance and data privacy emerge as terminal outcomes. All three analytical methods converge on a conclusion: agentic AI risks originate at the institutional layer, with technical risks acting as transmission mechanisms. Practical implications The findings indicate that effective governance requires that workforce capability, data integrity and objective-function alignment are addressed before deployment. The stratified agentic AI governance framework is proposed that translates hierarchical structure into a sequenced intervention architecture, providing practitioners with governance priorities organized by risk-propagation logic. Originality/value This paper contributes a systematically derived risk taxonomy and a causally weighted governance map for agentic AI risks in supply chains. Five propositions are derived from the causal structure and are advanced as a testable research agenda.

title: Visual Filters and Digital Subjectivity on Chinese Social Media: Platform Power, Beauty Labour, and Identity Negotiation
abstract: In the digital presentation of the self, visual filters can have a huge impact in Chinese social media on identity construction and expression, emotional expression, and social expectation negotiation. In this research, we will look at the double effect of the visual filters on Douyin and Xiaohongshu (Rednote) and how they (re)produce aesthetic standards and offer possibilities for individual agency. Taking on the qualitative case study approach, the three types of filtering - beautification filters connected to the "bai-you-shou" aesthetic, crying filters for an expression of emotions, and cartoon distortion filters for concealment of identity - are examined based on the theory of disciplinary power and technologies of the self and the theory of emotional capitalism and the theory of everyday tactics. The analysis shows that beautification filters are suitable for the function of self-surveillance and beautification work in the online space, and the emotional filters have an influence on the presentation and perception of emotion in an online space. Filters for concealment, on the other hand, offer other ways to work on issues of visibility and negotiate privacy. These practices show visual filters to not only be about platform control, but also not solely about personal empowerment. Rather, they must be comprehended within the dynamic between platform architecture and cultural norms and uses of the platform. This study integrates the aspects of aesthetic control, emotional expression and identity management of digital subjectivity to social media in the modern China, which enriches the research on digital subjectivity in China with a more sophisticated dimension.

title: The Introduction, Survival and Development of Public REITs in China
journal: Advances in Economics, Management and Political Sciences
abstract: Public real estate investment trusts provide a capital-market mechanism for converting income-producing assets into liquid and tradable investment vehicles. China launched its pilot programme for publicly offered infrastructure REITs in 2020, and the first nine products began trading on the Shanghai and Shenzhen Stock Exchanges on 21 June 2021, raising approximately RMB 31.4 billion. Over the subsequent five years the market evolved from a narrowly focused pilot into a multi-asset platform covering infrastructure, affordable rental housing, consumption facilities and commercial real estate. By mid-June 2026 the number of listed public REITs had reached 86, with cumulative capital raised of RMB 245 billion. Expansion offerings became operational, creating a dual mechanism of primary issuance and follow-on fundraising. This paper examines the policy origins, market expansion trajectory, operating performance and principal constraints facing Chinese public REITs. Drawing on exchange statistics, regulatory notices and secondary-market data, the analysis shows that the sector has achieved substantial scale and institutional completeness. Nevertheless, limited secondary-market liquidity, valuation dispersion across asset classes and an institutionally concentrated investor base continue to constrain market depth. Sustained development will depend on further improvements in market microstructure, operational transparency and investor diversification.

title: The Impact of Work–Life Balance and Organizational Support on Job Satisfaction: The Mediating Role of Psychological Well-Being
journal: Journal of Management, and Development Research
abstract: The present study attempts to examine the relationship between job satisfaction (JS) of bankers in Bangladesh and work-life balance (WLB) and organizational support (OS), with the mediating role of psychological well-being (PWB). Drawing on the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model, Work-Life Balance Theory, and Social Exchange Theory, the study provides a holistic understanding of how personal and organizational factors shape satisfaction differences in high-demand service environments. A cross-sectional quantitative survey was conducted using convenience sampling, with data collected from 201 bankers across 19 commercial banks in Bangladesh via a structured questionnaire. The data were analysed using confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modelling (SEM). Results show that WLB and OS have significant positive effects on PWB, which in turn has a positive effect on JS. The mediation analysis indicated that PWB partially mediated the relationship between WLB and JS, and also partially mediated the relationship between OS and JS. The findings emphasize the importance of psychological health in translating a positive work environment and work-life balance into job satisfaction. Theoretically, the study contributes to the research on WLB and OS by adding insights from the context of a developing country. Practically, it offers implications for HR managers aiming to implement interventions that boost employee satisfaction, engagement, and sustainable performance

Who stands with the virtual influencer? Trust in nonprofit versus corporate partnerships in social advocacy
journal: Journal of Research in Interactive Marketing
abstract: Purpose This research investigates whether collaborations between virtual influencers (VIs) and organizations can reduce consumers' perceptions of opportunism and cynicism in social advocacy. It further examines the mediating role of trust and whether vulnerability disclosure moderates these relationships. Design/methodology/approach Two preregistered experiments (N = 640) examined responses to social advocacy campaigns. Study 1 compared three conditions: a VI advocating alone, a VI collaborating with a company, and a VI collaborating with a nonprofit organization (NPO). Study 2 used a 2 × 2 design crossing collaboration type (VI-company vs. VI-NPO) with vulnerability disclosure (budget constraints disclosed vs. not disclosed) to test whether disclosure moderated the indirect effects through trust. Findings In Study 1, VI-NPO collaboration generated higher trust and lower opportunism and cynicism than VI-only advocacy, whereas the corresponding VI-company comparisons were not significant. Study 2 found the same nonprofit advantage over company collaboration. Trust mediated these differences in negative perceptions. Vulnerability disclosure reduced opportunism and cynicism but did not significantly increase trust or moderate the indirect effects through trust. Originality/value This research advances understanding of how organizational partnerships shape consumer responses to VIs in social advocacy. The findings highlight the importance of the organizational partner's identity and the role of trust in consumers' evaluations of advocacy actors. They also extend research on vulnerability disclosure by showing that acknowledging organizational constraints can reduce negative evaluations even when its proposed effects on trust are not supported.
